title: Effect of post-annealing temperature on the microstructure, texture, and mechanical properties of a deformed ferrite-martensite stainless steel
abstract: This research explores the impact of annealing on the microstructure, texture, and mechanical behavior of asymmetrically rolled dual-phase stainless steel. A dual-phase (ferrite-martensite) stainless steel sheet, 4 mm in thickness, underwent 60 % asymmetric cold rolling, followed by annealing at 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C for 30 min. The findings revealed that at 600 °C, partial recrystallization took place, while at 800 °C, complete recrystallization and martensite island decomposition were observed. The presence of martensite islands contributed to a highly uniform microstructure across both the near-surface and mid-thickness regions. Texture analysis showed that as the annealing temperature increased, α-fiber ({hkl}<110>) and γ-fiber ({111}<uvw>) textures became predominant. Mechanical tests demonstrated a reduction in macrohardness and microhardness with increasing annealing temperature. Tensile tests indicated a trade-off between decreasing strength and increasing ductility at higher annealing temperatures. Work hardening rate analysis suggested a smoother hardness reduction at elevated temperatures, attributed to enhanced strain accommodation resulting from martensite decomposition and a decrease in defect density. Fractographic analysis showed that fracture surfaces evolved from heterogeneous structures at lower temperatures to a fully ductile morphology at 800 °C, characterized by deeper and more uniformly distributed dimples, signifying improved microstructural homogeneity. Among the examined samples, the 600-30 specimen exhibited the most favorable mechanical properties owing to its superior combination of high strength (∼1 GPa) and good ductility (∼15 %).
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: AISI 430 ferritic stainless steels (FSSs) present a more cost-effective alternative to austenitic stainless steels, offering advantages such as a lower thermal expansion coefficient and enhanced resistance to pitting and stress corrosion. These properties make them more suitable for various applications where dimensional stability and corrosion resistance are critical [ 1–3 ]. AISI 430 ferritic stainless steels, when processed through conventional annealing, demonstrate excellent ductility but exhibit relatively low strength, restricting their application primarily to water heater liners, household appliances, appliance manufacturing, medical devices, and exhaust systems in automobiles. However, by employing an appropriate heat treatment strategy to enhance their mechanical strength, these steels could be utilized in a broader range of applications. Notably, they have the potential to replace conventional stainless steel components in automotive structural parts such as vehicle body construction [ 4–8 ]. In the automotive industry, galvanized steel sheets are widely used to improve corrosion resistance. This typically involves processes such as hot-dip galvanizing or sulfate zinc plating, which, despite their effectiveness, generate substantial environmental pollutants due to the release of hazardous chemicals and byproducts [ 9 , 10 ]. An alternative solution is AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel, which possesses excellent intrinsic corrosion resistance, eliminating the need for such protective treatments and thereby reducing environmental impact.

Extensive research has explored strategies to enhance the mechanical properties and formability of AISI 430 FSS by cold rolling and annealing. Meng et al. [ 11 ] investigated the effect of combining recrystallization annealing with quenching and partitioning (Q&P) on AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel. This treatment enhanced both strength and plasticity compared to conventional annealing by forming a microstructure of ferrite, martensite, and retained austenite. The improved mechanical properties make the material more suitable for automotive structural applications. Yang et al. [ 12 ] examined how variations in intercritical annealing temperature and duration affect the microstructural evolution and tensile performance of a newly designed medium-Mn steel. Their study revealed that this thermal treatment plays a key role in controlling the amount and stability of retained austenite, which in turn enhances the material's tensile properties. The optimized process resulted in a strength-ductility product reaching 1.5 times, demonstrating superior mechanical performance compared to Al-free 7Mn steels. The study on the influence of intermediate annealing on cold-rolled materials, which demonstrated a significant enhancement in the formability of ferritic stainless steel sheets, was conducted by Huh and Engler [ 13 ]. Their study demonstrated that annealing modifies the material's crystallographic texture by promoting a more pronounced yet less intense BCC rolling texture while minimizing texture gradient variations. These changes contribute to improved workability and better mechanical performance in forming applications.

Gao et al. [ 14 ] conducted a comparative study of two cold-rolling strategies on ferritic stainless steel to examine their impact on through-thickness texture evolution and grain colony arrangement, with the aim of improving deep drawing capabilities. The two-stage cold-rolling process was found to promote a more uniform gamma-fiber recrystallization texture and a homogeneous distribution of grain colonies, ultimately leading to superior deep drawability compared to the conventional single-stage approach. This suggests a refined control over microstructural features through the two-step process. Wang et al. [ 15 ] investigated the manipulation of cold-rolling parameters to tailor the recrystallization texture and mitigate surface ridging in AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel. Their analysis revealed that a single-pass rolling and annealing regime led to an enhancement of the γ-fiber texture component. Conversely, a dual-stage rolling process effectively engineered a more typical BCC texture with a broadened grain orientation distribution, resulting in a significant reduction in surface ridging susceptibility. Notably, cross-rolling induced a recrystallization texture dominated by specific {100} and {111}<uvw> crystallographic components. The implementation of an intermediate annealing step further refined the orientation alignment, thereby promoting the development of a desired BCC texture conducive to improved surface quality. The study on the kinetic aspects of recrystallization in Fe–19Cr–2Mo–Nb–Ti ferritic stainless steel, which involved analyzing the microstructure and texture evolution as a function of annealing temperature, was conducted by Cai et al. [ 16 ]. Their research elucidated that in-grain shear bands, generated through cold rolling, functioned as preferential nucleation sites for γ-fiber-oriented grains. This mechanism promoted the formation of a uniform, equiaxed grain morphology under optimized annealing conditions, which directly influenced the material's formability. Specifically, an annealing temperature of 1050 °C significantly augmented the nucleation rate of γ-fiber-oriented grains, leading to a substantial enhancement in formability characteristics. Ma et al. [ 17 ] undertook a comparative investigation into the differential response of 430 and 430LR ferritic stainless steels to varying rolling and annealing regimes, with a specific focus on elucidating the mechanisms governing ridging formation. Their findings revealed that 430LR exhibited a significantly diminished susceptibility to ridging, a phenomenon directly attributable to a refined microstructural architecture and a precisely tailored crystallographic texture. This resulted in a quantifiable 30 % reduction in ridging height compared to the 430 variant. The suppression of coarse banding and the elimination of grains possessing {001} crystallographic orientations were identified as pivotal factors in conferring enhanced ridging resistance across both material grades. The study on the impact of martensite on ferritic stainless steel properties was conducted by Lu et al. [ 18 ]. They found that annealing above 900 °C followed by water quenching forms martensite along ferrite grain boundaries, leading to increased hardness and strength but reduced ductility. Luo et al. [ 19 ] examined the effects of the quenching and partitioning process on the microstructure and mechanical properties of ferritic stainless steel. Their findings highlighted that the incorporation of martensite within the microstructure significantly enhances the material's strength. The study on the effect of pre-cold-rolling martensite on the annealed microstructure of ferritic stainless steel after cold rolling was conducted by Kimura et al. [ 20 ]. A key finding of their study was the formation of curved ferrite grains surrounding the martensite phase, attributed to strain introduced during the cold rolling process. Also, placing martensite islands at different temperatures leads to changes in the hardness of the martensite islands themselves. Kaneko et al. [ 21 ] pioneered a novel processing paradigm for the production of thin steel strips, leveraging multipass groove rolling to achieve targeted crystallographic texture engineering. Their investigation elucidated that the application of spread rolling resulted in a marked augmentation of the γ-fiber texture component, coupled with a concomitant attenuation of the α-fiber texture, relative to conventionally flat-rolled materials. This controlled textural transformation engendered a significant reduction in planar anisotropy. Furthermore, it was observed that the implementation of post-deformation annealing protocols led to a progressive diminishment of the overall crystallographic texture intensity. The traditional bell furnace annealing process helps retain the plasticity of AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel; however, it leads to insufficient strength, significantly limiting its practical applications. To enhance processing efficiency by minimizing annealing duration, reducing energy consumption, and maintaining the original chemical composition, our research group has conducted an in-depth investigation into the microstructural transformations and mechanical properties of AISI 430 FSS after undergoing intercritical annealing within the two-phase (α+γ) region and performing asymmetric rolling [ 22 ].

Ding et al. [ 23 ] explored the efficacy of asymmetric rolling (ASR) in achieving grain refinement within commercial-purity iron. Their investigation demonstrated the development of equiaxed ultrafine grains, with an average size of approximately 0.9 μm, characterized by a substantial proportion of high-angle grain boundaries. This microstructural evolution was attributed to the introduction of supplementary shear strain during the ASR process. The resulting microstructure conferred enhanced yield strength and elevated microhardness, while exhibiting a diminished work hardening capacity, attributed to the high dislocation density and distinctive grain boundary characteristics. The study on the impact of differential speed rolling on the mitigation of surface ridging and the evolution of crystallographic texture in ultra-purified 17 %Cr ferritic stainless steel was conducted by Lu et al. [ 24 ]. Their findings revealed that conventional cold rolling induced significant ridging, attributed to the formation of band-like aggregates of γ-fiber (<111>//ND) grains. In contrast, differential speed rolling, especially at elevated speed ratios, effectively diminished ridging depth and enhanced surface quality. The introduction of shear bands during asymmetric deformation facilitated recrystallization, disrupting the band-like grain clusters and promoting a more randomized grain orientation distribution. Lu et al. [ 25 ] conducted a comparative investigation into the influence of conventional and asymmetric rolling techniques on texture evolution and surface ridging resistance in ultra-pure 17 % chromium ferritic stainless steel. Their research elucidated that conventional rolling induced heterogeneous deformation and substantial texture gradients, thereby compromising ridging resistance. Conversely, asymmetric rolling facilitated homogeneous shear deformation, resulting in the formation of uniform recrystallized grains and a randomized crystallographic orientation distribution, leading to a significant enhancement in ridging resistance. These findings underscore that texture gradients and orientation inhomogeneity are a direct consequence of non-uniform deformation, while asymmetric rolling effectively mitigates these effects through the generation of shear bands and a uniform orientation gradient across the sheet thickness.

Although previous studies have investigated the effects of asymmetric rolling on ridging in ferritic stainless steel, as well as the influence of conventional cold rolling followed by annealing on its mechanical properties, these works exhibit notable shortcomings. Specifically, they did not adequately address the combined impact of asymmetric rolling and subsequent annealing on the material's mechanical behavior, microstructure, and crystallographic texture. Moreover, the effect of annealing on asymmetrically rolled AISI 430 alloy has not been clearly elucidated, leaving gaps in understanding how annealing influences microstructural evolution, texture development, and overall performance in this specific processing route. This study examines how different annealing temperatures affect the microstructure, texture, and mechanical properties of ferritic stainless steel after 60 % asymmetric cold rolling.

sections.heading: Experimental procedure
paragraphs:
A 4 mm thick AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel sheet, with its chemical composition detailed in  Table 1 
                      , was used as the initial material. To achieve a two-phase microstructure, the sheets were annealed at 950 °C for 6 h, followed by water quenching. The asymmetric rolling process employed a single-roll drive system, where the lower roller maintained a constant rotational speed of 3.2 rpm, while the upper roller was driven by friction. The rollers measured 150 mm in diameter and 200 mm in width. A total reduction of 60 % was applied during asymmetric cold rolling. The deformed samples were subsequently annealed at 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C. The heat treatment procedure, with terminology conforming to ASTM  A941 ,  involved  holding the samples at the target temperature for 30 min, followed by air cooling to room temperature. These annealed samples were designated as 600-30, 700-30, and 800-30, respectively.

The preparation of samples for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis was conducted using a Struers Tegramin 20 system. Initial plane grinding was performed with 320-grit SiC paper, followed by fine grinding using a 9 μm DiaPro suspension applied to an MD Largo disc. Final polishing was carried out on an MD Chem cloth with an OP-S non-dry colloidal silica suspension for 30 min. EBSD measurements were performed using a ThermoFisher Helios G4 CXe PFIB-SEM equipped with an AMETEK HIKARI EBSD camera. The analysis was conducted at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV, a step size of 0.4 μm, and a beam current of 1.6 nA over a 200 × 200 μm 2  area on the steel samples. Post-processing of the acquired EBSD data was conducted using the ATEX software [ 26 ].

Macrohardness was evaluated using a Brinell hardness tester with an applied load of 10 kg. The reported hardness values represent the average of 11 measurements taken on both surfaces of the sheet along the rolling direction-transverse direction (RD-TD) plane. Microhardness was assessed using Vickers microhardness testing on the rolling direction-normal direction (RD-ND) plane. A 100 gf load was applied with a 200 μm indentation. To enhance measurement accuracy, the final microhardness values were determined by averaging three measurements taken along parallel lines in the normal direction.

Tensile testing was conducted at room temperature in accordance with the ASTM  E8 /E8M standard using a Santam universal testing machine at a constant crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. Total elongation was determined by measuring the change in gauge length after fracture. Fracture surface analysis was carried out using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to examine failure mechanisms.

sections.heading: Microstructural and textural evolutions
paragraphs:
The microstructures of the 60 % deformed sample were shown in previous work [ 22 ].  Figs. 1 and 2 
                         
                          depict the image quality (IQ) and orientation maps of partially annealed specimens, highlighting microstructural features in the near-surface and mid-thickness regions. As presented in  Fig. 1 (a) and (b), the microstructure of the 600-30 sample is characterized by martensite islands, curved ferrite grains, and zigzag deformation bands oriented along the rolling direction. In addition to the presence of zigzag bands, the microstructure of the 600-30 sample also exhibits shear and deformation bands, indicating that annealing at 600 °C primarily facilitated dynamic recovery, with only limited recrystallization occurring. According to  Figs. 1 and 2 , the near-surface and mid-thickness regions of the 600-30 sample exhibit distinct characteristics. In certain areas near the surface, due to partial decarburization, the number of martensite islands is lower than in other regions. This reduction leads to more elongated grains and a higher density of shear and deformation bands, rather than curved ferrite grains and zigzag bands, as observed in the mid-thickness region. Additionally, the increased shear strain near the surface acts as a driving force for the observed microstructural differences. Crystalline defects and high-energy regions, such as zigzag bands and the interfaces between martensite islands and ferrite grains, are recognized as preferential sites for the nucleation of new grains during recrystallization [ 27–30 ].  Fig. 2 (a) and (b) reveal that the grain nucleation predominantly occurs at deformation bands, martensite-ferrite interfaces, and zigzag bands. These regions exhibit a higher concentration of nucleation sites both within their structure and in their vicinity [ 31 , 32 ].

Fig. 1(c), (d), 2(c), and 2(d)  illustrate the microstructural evolution of the 700-30 sample in both the near-surface and mid-thickness regions. The 100 °C increase in annealing temperature has not led to drastic structural modifications; however, a significant decrease in the density of zigzag, shear, and deformation bands is evident. The martensite islands in the 700-30 sample appear smaller than those in the 600-30 sample, likely due to decomposition. Furthermore, a higher number of recrystallized grains is observed in the 700-30 sample. These observations suggest that, although still limited, recovery and recrystallization have progressed more extensively in the 700-30 sample compared to the 600-30 sample.

As shown in  Fig. 1 (e) and (f), the microstructural analysis of the 800-30 sample confirms the occurrence of full recrystallization. A key characteristic of this sample is the complete disappearance of martensite islands from the microstructure. Previous research on martensite recrystallization suggests that quenched martensite exhibits significant resistance to recrystallization. However, when subjected to plastic deformation, such as cold rolling, martensite undergoes recrystallization more readily. Moreover, as the degree of plastic deformation increases, the temperature required for recrystallization decreases [ 33 ]. Due to the asymmetric rolling process and the additional shear strain applied to the sample, the necessary driving force for the decomposition of martensite islands at 800 °C was provided, resulting in their complete elimination. In addition to the disappearance of martensite islands, zigzag bands, deformation bands, shear bands, and curved grains were also removed, giving way to strain-free, equiaxed recrystallized grains. Furthermore, no significant microstructural differences were observed between the near-surface and mid-thickness regions of the 800-30 sample, with the grain sizes measured at 12.2 μm and 12.7 μm, respectively. Overall, the presence of martensite islands in the rolled sample's microstructure contributed to maintaining uniform grain morphology and a homogeneous microstructure throughout the entire thickness.

To provide a more comprehensive evaluation,  Figs. 3 and 4 
                         
                          display the grain orientation spread (GOS) and recrystallization (RX) maps of the samples. Furthermore,  Table 2 
                          presents a summary of the recrystallized area fractions of all samples. Analysis of  Figs. 3 and 4  reveals that the 600-30 sample mainly underwent recovery, with only a limited extent of recrystallization. The recrystallized regions are primarily concentrated around high-energy sites, including the interfaces between martensite islands and ferrite, as well as within zigzag, shear, and deformation bands. The GOS and recrystallization (RX) maps reveal distinct differences in microstructural behavior between the near-surface and mid-thickness regions of the sample. As previously discussed, the strain distribution varies across these regions, with the near-surface area experiencing a higher density of dislocations, defects, and deformation bands. Nevertheless, the presence of martensite islands has facilitated the formation of high-energy regions, particularly at martensite-ferrite interfaces, consistently throughout the sample thickness.  Fig. 3 (a) and (b) indicate that the majority of new grains nucleated at these interfaces, with additional grain formation also occurring within some martensite islands. Overall, martensite islands have played a crucial role in promoting uniform recovery and recrystallization across different regions. The recrystallized area fraction in the mid-thickness of the 600-30 sample is 3 %, while in the near-surface region, it is slightly lower (2.9 %). Following annealing at 700 °C, an enhanced degree of static recovery was observed in both the mid-thickness ( Fig. 4 (c)) and near-surface ( Fig. 4 (d)) regions. Despite this, the extent of recrystallization remained relatively low. The recrystallized area fraction was determined to be 13.7 % in the mid-thickness and 10.4 % in the near-surface region, confirming the limited progression of recrystallization within the sample. A comparison of the GOS and RX maps between the 700-30 and 600-30 samples reveals that the extent of recrystallization is significantly greater in the 700-30 sample, primarily due to the higher annealing temperature. On average, the recrystallized area fraction in the 700-30 sample is nearly four times larger than that in the 600-30 sample. Moreover, an increased presence of recrystallized grains is observed within the martensite islands. At an annealing temperature of 800 °C, recrystallization has been fully achieved. The GOS maps of the 800-30 sample, presented in  Fig. 3 (e) and (f), demonstrate microstructural similarity between the mid-thickness and near-surface regions. Furthermore, the RX maps ( Fig. 4 (e) and (f)) confirm the completion of the recrystallization process. As indicated in  Table 2 , the recrystallized area fraction in the 800-30 sample is 93.3 % in the near-surface region and 89.9 % in the mid-thickness region. The final grain size after recrystallization is generally determined by factors such as the initial grain size, annealing conditions (temperature and duration), and the degree of pre-strain applied. Given the substantial strain induced by asymmetric cold rolling and the annealing temperature of 800 °C, a higher density of newly formed grains has developed, leading to a highly uniform microstructure across the entire thickness of the 800-30 sample.

For a more detailed investigation,  Figs. 5 and 6 
                         
                          illustrate the Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM) maps and the distribution of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density at various annealing temperatures. Unlike GOS maps, which primarily detect high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) by measuring angular variations between adjacent pixels, KAM evaluates local misorientations at a finer scale. This approach enables the identification of both deformed regions and recrystallized areas within individual grains. As reported by Reip et al. [ 34 ], KAM serves as a quantitative indicator of stored energy by representing dislocation density and visualizing the distribution of crystalline defects. While KAM captures localized misorientations, GOS characterizes broader orientation gradients, offering insight into the overall microstructural homogeneity.  Fig. 5 (a) and (b) demonstrate that the 600-30 sample has undergone recovery, as evidenced by the relatively low KAM values in numerous grains. This reduction implies a decrease in dislocation density and stored strain energy resulting from annealing at 600 °C. Nevertheless, a more detailed examination reveals elevated KAM values concentrated around the interfaces between martensite islands and ferrite, as well as within the zigzag bands. Under intense asymmetric cold rolling, dislocations tend to concentrate more densely around martensite islands than within ferrite grains. The boundaries between martensite islands and ferrites function as preferential sites for dislocation accumulation, facilitating the initiation and development of recrystallized grains. Moreover, zigzag bands formed during deformation, characterized by high misorientation, along with grain boundaries, provide suitable locations for recrystallization nucleation [ 35 ]. Furthermore, low KAM values indicate the presence of recrystallized nuclei around shear bands in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions. The KAM maps confirm that the 600-30 sample has undergone partial recovery and limited recrystallization. Additionally, regions with high KAM values, including grain boundaries and deformation bands, are clearly identified in both the mid-thickness and near-surface areas as favorable sites for the nucleation of new recrystallized grains.  Fig. 5 (c) and (d) display the KAM maps for the 700-30 sample, revealing an overall reduction in KAM values compared to the 600-30 sample. This decline is attributed to the increased recrystallization in the 700-30 sample, which has led to a significant decrease in dislocation density. Nevertheless, localized regions with elevated KAM values remain visible around certain martensite islands. A comparison between  Fig. 5(c) and (d) and Fig. 5(a) and (b)  suggests that the microstructure of the 700-30 sample is more homogeneous in terms of dislocation density and KAM distribution across both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions than that of the 600-30 sample.

The KAM maps for the 800-30 sample demonstrate that full recrystallization has substantially lowered dislocation density in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions, as evidenced by the predominantly low KAM values in the microstructure. A strong correlation exists between KAM values and geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density, where higher KAM values indicate increased misorientation between adjacent areas, leading to a greater accumulation of GNDs [ 20 ]. According to  Fig. 6 , the 600-30 sample has the highest GND density, particularly in the near-surface region, which is likely due to the intense shear strain imposed by asymmetric rolling. With increasing annealing temperature, the GND density decreases in both regions, resulting in a more homogeneous GND distribution throughout the thickness of the sample.

The microtexture analysis of the post-annealed samples at various temperatures is depicted in  Fig. 7 
                         , highlighting the differences between the near-surface and mid-thickness regions.  Fig. 7 (a) and (b) display the texture of the 600-30 sample, revealing the presence of both deformation and shear textures in both regions. Despite this similarity, noticeable distinctions exist between the near-surface and mid-thickness areas. As depicted in  Fig. 7 (a), the 600-30 sample exhibits a shear-related Rotated Cube component at the φ 2  = 0° and φ 2  = 45° sections, with an intensity of approximately 2.1 × R. This texture coexists with the α-fiber component, where <110> aligns with the rolling direction. The dominant texture in this sample is the ({112}<110>) component, part of the α-fiber, which reaches an intensity of around 4.7 × R. These results align with previous studies [ 36 ], demonstrating that a 60 % thickness reduction via asymmetric rolling promotes the development of a pronounced deformation and shear texture. Overall, deformation in ferritic stainless steels typically results in the formation of α-fiber and γ-fiber textures [ 37 , 38 ]. As indicated by the microstructure of the 600-30 sample in the mid-thickness region ( Fig. 1 (a)) and the recrystallized area fraction ( Table 2 ), the limited recrystallization and dominant recovery process preserved the texture components of the 60 % cold-rolled sample after annealing at 600 °C with minimal alteration. The texture analysis of the near-surface region, shown in  Fig. 7 (b), reveals a pronounced Rotated Cube component with an intensity of approximately 5.4 × R. Furthermore, a relatively strong α-fiber texture and a weaker γ-fiber texture are also observed.  Fig. 7 (a) and (b) indicate that the Rotated Cube (shear) component exhibits significantly greater intensity in the near-surface region than in the mid-thickness region. Since the recrystallized area fractions are nearly identical in both regions, this difference is primarily linked to the distinct strain characteristics experienced by the near-surface layers compared to the interior. In general, shear components tend to be more pronounced near the surface than in the mid-thickness area. Moreover, the near-surface region displays a weak γ-fiber texture, while the mid-thickness region exhibits both a weak γ-fiber texture and a dominant α-fiber texture. These variations result from differences in the applied strain during the rolling process. This finding is consistent with the results of deformation induced by asymmetric rolling in ferritic stainless steels [ 25 ]. In the mid-thickness region, due to the plane strain conditions, the deformed texture is different from that near the surface. In general, the regions near the center intensify the plane strain more, which leads to the formation of a stronger α-fiber texture in these regions [ 39 ].

The ODF map of the mid-thickness region in the 700-30 sample ( Fig. 7 (c)) indicates that annealing at 700 °C has had minimal impact on the Rotated Cube component. One key difference in the mid-thickness texture of the 700-30 sample compared to the 600-30 sample is the decrease in the {112}<110> component intensity within the α-fiber, accompanied by an increase in γ-fiber components. Specifically, the {112}<110> component intensity has dropped from nearly 4.7 × R to 2.8 × R. At the same time, γ-fiber components such as {111}<112> and {111}<011> appear with an intensity of approximately 2.8 × R. Additionally, the {554}<225> component is present with an intensity of about 3.2 × R. In general, raising the annealing temperature by 100 °C has facilitated the rotation of grain orientations. As shown in  Fig. 7 (d), the near-surface region of the 700-30 sample exhibits weak Rotated Cube components. A key distinction between the near-surface texture of the 700-30 and 600-30 samples is the approximately 40° rotation of the α-fiber component from the Rotated Cube along the φ axis, accompanied by a significant increase in the intensity of the {112}<110> component, reaching 6.7 × R. Additionally, γ-fiber-related components are prominently observed near the surface of this sample. A comparative analysis of the near-surface microtexture between the 700-30 and 600-30 samples reveals that annealing at a 100 °C higher temperature facilitates the transition of α-fiber components to γ-fiber components throughout the thickness while inducing a shift from the Rotated Cube component to α-fiber components near the surface. In ferritic stainless steels with a BCC crystal structure, the γ-fiber is generally associated with recrystallization, although its formation can also occur during deformation [ 18 , 34 , 38 , 40 ]. The general path of γ-to-α fiber rotation is as follows [ 41 , 42 ]: 
                            
                               {001}<110> → {115}<110> → {114}<110> → {113}<110> →{112}<110> → {223}<110> → {111}<110> → {111}<112> → {111}<011>

As depicted in  Fig. 7 (e), the mid-thickness region of the 800-30 sample exhibits the formation of an α-fiber texture with {112}<110> orientation and a γ-fiber texture with {111}<112> orientation, both possessing an intensity of 4.6 × R. Analyzing the texture development in the mid-thickness region of the 600-30, 700-30, and 800-30 samples reveals that annealing of the 60 % cold-rolled specimen led to grain rotation throughout the recrystallization process, progressing according to the identified sequence. Specifically, in the 600-30 sample, the mid-thickness texture was initially close to the Rotated Cube component. However, with a 100 °C increase in annealing temperature, it transformed into a strengthened {111}<112> component along with γ-fiber and the {112}<110> component. At 800 °C, the {111}<112> component reached its maximum intensity, while the intensity of the Rotated Cube shear texture significantly decreased in the 700-30 and 800-30 samples. The Rotated Cube shear texture, which was prominent in the mid-thickness region of the 600-30 sample, was substantially weakened in the 800-30 sample due to sufficient recrystallization, leading to an enhancement of the γ-fiber texture.  Fig. 7 (f) illustrates the microtexture of the 800-30 sample in the near-surface region. A comparison with the 700-30 sample reveals that following the γ-to-α fiber transition observed in the 700-30 sample, the α-fiber in the 800-30 sample further evolved into the Cube component. Moreover, the intensity of the Goss texture component showed a notable increase. The variation in the final texture of the 800-30 sample between the near-surface and mid-thickness regions is primarily linked to differences in the initial texture of the 600-30 sample, variations in applied shear strain, and the absence of lubrication during rolling. In the 600-30 sample, the shear texture near the surface is more pronounced compared to the mid-thickness region. As a result, the transformation of texture components from α-fiber (indicative of deformation) to γ-fiber (associated with recrystallization) occurs at a slower rate in the near-surface regions than in the mid-thickness regions. In contrast, the 800-30 sample exhibits substantial γ-fiber formation across both thickness regions. Overall, the presence of martensite islands in the microstructure of the rolled samples facilitated the development of a relatively homogeneous texture after annealing. This conclusion aligns with findings reported in a previous study [ 43 ].

Fig. 8 
                          presents the misorientation distribution of AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel after annealing at different temperatures. In the 600-30 samples, ferrite grains and zigzag bands are mainly associated with high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), whereas martensite-ferrite interfaces and the interior of martensite islands exhibit a predominance of low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs). This distribution pattern is linked to subgrain formation during cold rolling, followed by recovery at 600 °C [ 4 ]. The proportion of LAGBs in the mid-thickness and near-surface regions is measured at 51.8 % and 49.9 %, respectively. In the 700-30 sample, LAGBs remain prominent within the martensite islands, with no significant reduction observed. The LAGB fractions in the mid-thickness and near-surface regions are measured at 43.4 % and 45.5 %, respectively, indicating minimal change compared to the 600-30 sample. This finding is consistent with the limited recrystallization progression at this temperature. Upon increasing the annealing temperature to 800 °C, the proportion of HAGBs increases, signifying advanced recrystallization and the formation of a more uniform microstructure, in agreement with previous studies [ 44 ]. The decomposition of martensite islands and the formation of new ferrite grains lead to the transformation of many LAGBs into HAGBs. Consequently, extensive recrystallization significantly lowers the LAGB fraction in the mid-thickness and near-surface regions of the 800-30 sample to 16.5 % and 16.7 %, respectively, marking a notable decrease compared to the 600-30 and 700-30 samples. Moreover, the negligible variation in LAGB fractions between the analyzed regions across different samples reinforces the conclusion that the presence of martensite in the initial microstructure before asymmetric rolling enhances microstructural homogeneity after annealing.

Fig. 9 
                          illustrates the CSL boundary distribution in the annealed samples. During recrystallization, special boundaries like CSL boundaries develop as the material strives to lower its overall energy. Due to their more structured atomic arrangement relative to high-angle and randomly oriented grain boundaries, CSL boundaries contribute to reduced boundary energy and improved microstructural stability. Σ3 boundaries, known for their low energy and restricted mobility, are essential in the development of texture during rolling and annealing. These boundaries emerge through grain rotation and are closely linked to recrystallization and recovery mechanisms. Notably, there is a strong relationship between Σ3 boundaries and γ-fiber textures ({111}<112> and {111}<110>), which result from a 30-degree rotation around the ⟨111⟩ axis. As annealing progresses, the proportion of Σ3 boundaries steadily rises, highlighting their importance in stabilizing the recrystallized microstructure and promoting a more uniform texture. Σ13b boundaries, which develop through a distinct 27.8-degree rotation around the ⟨111⟩ axis, are closely linked to γ-fiber texture components. Their growing presence throughout rolling and sequential annealing indicates their role in reinforcing {111}<112> and {111}<110> texture components. The rise in Σ13b boundary fractions is attributed to grain rearrangement and alignment during recovery and recrystallization, which enhances the overall stability of the microstructure. Other boundaries, such as Σ9 (characterized by a 38.9° misorientation around the ⟨110⟩ axis) and Σ11, are closely linked to recrystallized grains and are strongly affected by temperature variations. The fraction of these boundaries generally increases with annealing, especially at elevated temperatures, facilitating the development of stable textures. By improving grain boundary mobility, these boundaries accelerate recrystallization processes [ 45 , 46 ]. Moreover, Σ11 boundaries show a notable association with the presence of martensite islands. The occurrence of martensite islands significantly raises the probability of Σ11 boundary formation [ 47 ].

As illustrated in  Fig. 9 , Σ3, Σ11, and Σ13b boundaries exhibit more significant changes with temperature compared to other CSL boundaries. The fractions of Σ3 and Σ13b boundaries progressively increase with rising annealing temperatures, whereas Σ11 boundaries initially show an increase but subsequently decline at higher temperatures. For the 600-30 sample, Σ3 boundary fractions in the mid-thickness and near-surface regions are measured at 1.5 % and 1.4 %, respectively. When the annealing temperature reaches 700 °C, these values rise to 2.4 % in both regions. On average, the Σ3 boundary fraction in the 700-30 sample is 50 % greater than that in the 600-30 sample. This increase is primarily driven by recrystallization, which facilitates the formation of well-ordered grain boundaries while reducing the overall stored energy within the sample. Moreover, the Σ3 boundary fraction in the 800-30 sample is measured at 3.8 % in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions. The higher Σ3 fraction in the 800-30 sample compared to the 700-30 sample can be attributed to the development of a more pronounced γ-fiber texture in the mid-thickness region, along with the decomposition of martensite islands and their subsequent transformation into recrystallized ferrite grains. A similar trend is observed in the Σ13b boundary fraction. These results align well with the microtexture analysis findings. Conversely, in the 600-30 sample, Σ11 boundary fractions are recorded at 3.4 % in the mid-thickness region and 3.7 % in the near-surface region. With an increase in annealing temperature, these values rise in the 700-30 sample to 4.3 % and 4.4 % in the mid-thickness and near-surface regions, respectively, confirming a temperature-dependent increase in Σ11 boundaries.

A comparative analysis of Σ11 and Σ3 boundaries between the 600-30 and 700-30 samples reveals that the Σ3 fraction experiences a more substantial increase. This disparity is attributed to the distinct formation mechanisms of these boundaries. The growth of Σ3 boundaries is linked to the strengthening of {111}<112> and {111}<110> texture components, whereas Σ11 boundaries are directly correlated with the presence of martensite islands. The pronounced γ-fiber texture in the 700-30 sample, coupled with minimal changes in martensite island morphology, explains the divergence in the growth trends of Σ3 and Σ11 boundaries. In contrast, the Σ11 boundary fraction in the 800-30 sample decreases to 2 % in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions, averaging less than half of the fraction found in the 700-30 sample. As previously discussed, the extensive recrystallization and decomposition of martensite islands in the 800-30 sample result in a notable reduction in the fraction of Σ11 boundaries.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 10 
                          illustrates the macrohardness values for the initial, rolled, and annealed samples on both the upper and lower surfaces. The reason for assessing hardness on both surfaces is the use of asymmetric rolling, where stress is applied solely by the lower roll. Consequently, the upper and lower surfaces experience different levels of shear strain [ 28 , 29 , 48 , 49 ].  Fig. 10  illustrates that in the initial sample, the hardness values of the upper and lower surfaces are nearly the same. However, following the rolling process, the lower surface exhibits a higher hardness level than the upper surface, primarily due to the greater strain energy accumulated from the increased strain near the lower roll. Upon annealing at various temperatures, the hardness difference between the upper and lower surfaces undergoes noticeable changes. Generally, as the annealing temperature rises, this disparity diminishes. In the rolled sample, the lower surface hardness is 5 % higher than that of the upper surface. With annealing at 600 °C, where recovery and partial recrystallization occur, this difference decreases to 5 %. In the 700-30 and 800-30 samples, it is further reduced to 2.7 % and 0.3 %, respectively. These findings confirm that complete recrystallization, as depicted in  Fig. 2 , promotes microstructural homogeneity throughout the sheet thickness. As a result, in the 800-30 sample, there is practically no significant variation in hardness between the upper and lower surfaces.

The initial sample exhibits an average hardness of 190.7 HB, which rises to 304.0 HB after rolling. This 59 % increase in hardness results from asymmetric rolling, leading to a higher accumulation of defects such as dislocations, deformation bands, and zigzag structures. However, annealing progressively reduces the hardness, with average values measured at 297.7 HB for the 600-30 sample, 214.4 HB for the 700-30 sample, and 191.1 HB for the 800-30 sample. Compared to the initial sample, the 600-30, 700-30, and 800-30 samples demonstrated increases in average hardness of 56.1 %, 12.4 %, and 0.2 %, respectively. However, when compared to the rolled sample, the 600-30 sample exhibited a slight 2.1 % decrease in hardness, which can be attributed to the effects of recovery and limited recrystallization. In contrast, the 700-30 sample showed a 29.5 % reduction in hardness relative to the rolled sample, primarily due to recovery and the softening of martensite islands upon annealing at 700 °C. The 800-30 sample exhibited an even greater decrease of 37.1 %, indicating the substantial impact of widespread recrystallization and the decomposition of martensite islands. Furthermore,  Figs. 5 and 6  indicate a notable reduction in dislocation density in the 700-30 and 800-30 samples compared to the 600-30 sample. Consequently, it can be inferred that the substantial decrease in average hardness in the annealed samples, relative to the rolled sample, is primarily attributed to recrystallization and the development of newly formed, strain-free ferrite grains.

Fig. 11 
                          illustrates the microhardness values for the initial, rolled, and annealed sheets. The microhardness measurements revealed a uniform hardness distribution throughout the thickness of the initial sample. However, following asymmetric rolling, the highest hardness was observed near the lower roll, attributed to the intensified shear strain in this region. Moving away from this surface, the hardness progressively declined. Differences in dislocation density and work hardening in the rolled sample led to an uneven hardness distribution across the sheet thickness. As the annealing temperature increased, the microhardness profile became more homogeneous. In the 600-30 sample, recovery and limited recrystallization resulted in reduced microhardness compared to the rolled sample, while also enhancing uniformity. With the onset of recrystallization in the 700-30 and 800-30 samples, hardness decreased further, and the microhardness distribution across the thickness became nearly uniform.

The engineering stress-strain curves for the initial, rolled, and annealed samples are depicted in  Fig. 12 
                         . The corresponding mechanical properties, such as ultimate tensile strength (UTS), yield strength (YS), total elongation (TE), and absorbed energy (tensile toughness), are presented in  Fig. 13 
                         .  Figs. 12 and 13  show that in the initial sample, YS, UTS, and TE were measured at 270.9 MPa, 433.9 MPa, and 50.4 %, respectively. In contrast, the rolled sample exhibited a significant increase in YS and UTS to 1044.2 MPa and 1066.8 MPa, while TE dropped to 9.2 %. As highlighted in our previous study [ 22 ], this substantial increase in strength and reduction in ductility primarily result from strain hardening and the presence of hard martensite islands. According to  Figs. 12 and 13 , the 600-30 sample recorded YS and UTS values of 921.5 MPa and 987.2 MPa, respectively. This corresponds to a 240.1 % rise in YS and a 122.3 % increase in UTS compared to the initial sample. Conversely, TE experienced a significant reduction, dropping from 50.4 % in the initial sample to 14.4 % in the 600-30 sample. The substantial strength enhancement in the 600-30 sample, relative to the initial sample, is primarily due to the increased dislocation density and the presence of hard martensite islands. Beyond their intrinsic hardness, these martensite islands also promote the formation of zigzag bands in the microstructure, which contribute to secondary hardening. Nevertheless, when compared to the rolled sample, the 600-30 sample exhibited an 11.7 % decrease in YS and a 7.4 % reduction in UTS. Meanwhile, TE showed a 5.2 % increase compared to the rolled sample. By analyzing the microstructures of the rolled and 600-30 samples ( Figs. 2 and 4 ), it is evident that annealing at a relatively low temperature of 600 °C resulted in minimal recovery and recrystallization, leading to negligible changes in grain morphology and size between the two samples. Additionally, zigzag bands are present in both microstructures. However, the recovery process at this temperature contributed to a reduction in dislocation density. Consequently, the primary factor behind the decrease in strength and the improvement in ductility of the 600-30 sample relative to the rolled sample is the reduction in dislocation density due to static recovery.

As shown in  Fig. 13 , the 700-30 sample exhibits YS, UTS, and TE values of 597.3 MPa, 699.5 MPa, and 15.8 %, respectively. This represents an increase of 120.4 % in YS and 57.8 % in UTS compared to the initial sample.  Figs. 1–4  suggest that only partial recrystallization has occurred, indicating that the process has not fully progressed, likely resulting in a higher dislocation density in the 700-30 sample. Furthermore, rolling has significantly refined the grain size and reduced grain width. Consequently, the enhanced strength of the 700-30 sample, in comparison to the initial sample, can primarily be attributed to its finer grain structure and elevated dislocation density. A comparison of the engineering stress-strain curves indicates that the 700-30 sample exhibits a 42.7 % decrease in UTS and a 34.4 % decrease in YS compared to the rolled sample. This decline in strength is primarily attributed to a significant reduction in dislocation density due to recrystallization. Furthermore, since the sample was annealed at 700 °C, it is likely that the hardness of the martensite islands was affected at this temperature.

Kimura et al. [ 20 ] previously reported that exposing martensite islands to varying temperatures results in the tempering of martensite within the microstructure of ferritic stainless steel. Based on this, it can be inferred that subjecting the sample to 700 °C for 30 min led to the partial decomposition of martensite islands, consequently reducing their hardness compared to the rolled sample. The decrease in martensite island hardness is a key factor in the overall reduction in the strength of the 700-30 sample relative to the rolled sample. Increasing the annealing temperature from 600 °C to 700 °C led to a 35.1 % reduction in YS and a 34.4 % decline in UTS. Meanwhile, TE showed an increase from 14.4 % in the 600-30 sample to 15.8 % in the 700-30 sample. In general, the factors contributing to the decrease in strength in the 700-30 sample relative to the 600-30 sample are similar to those observed in comparison to the rolled sample. Although the 100 °C rise in annealing temperature did not result in extensive recrystallization, the recrystallized fraction in the 700-30 sample was nearly three times greater than that of the 600-30 sample, signifying a reduction in dislocation density. Additionally, as discussed earlier, annealing at 700 °C led to the softening of the rolled martensite islands, which significantly contributed to the observed decrease in hardness and strength in this sample.

Beyond these parameters, crystallographic texture and the Schmidt Factor play a crucial role in determining the mechanical properties of materials.  Fig. 14 
                          illustrates the Schmidt Factor distributions for the 600-30, 700-30, and 800-30 samples, highlighting variations in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions for the dominant slip systems ({110}<111>, {112}<111>, and {123}<111>) within the BCC structure. In AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel, slip systems with higher Schmidt Factors (SF) are more readily activated under applied stress due to the favorable orientation between the stress and slip directions. During plastic deformation, grains with elevated SF values initiate dislocation motion earlier, facilitating the propagation and multiplication of dislocations along specific crystallographic planes. Grains with high Schmidt Factors tend to slip more easily, contributing to a decrease in yield strength. In contrast, grains with lower Schmidt Factors resist slip system activation, enhancing material strength but reducing ductility. The interaction between these grain behaviors under stress plays a key role in defining the mechanical properties and functional performance of the material [ 50 ]. As shown in  Fig. 14 , the fraction of soft grains with high Schmidt Factors tends to increase as the annealing temperature rises. These grains are more likely to be activated during plastic deformation. As a result, the 700-30 sample contains a higher proportion of soft grains with high Schmidt Factors compared to the 600-30 sample. This increase, along with a reduction in dislocation density and the softening of martensite islands, plays a significant role in lowering the material's strength at a temperature of 700 °C.

As illustrated in  Fig. 13 , the 800-30 sample exhibits YS, UTS, and TE values of 263.9 MPa, 463.7 MPa, and 42.9 %, respectively, reflecting a slight 2.5 % reduction in YS and a modest 4.4 % increase in UTS relative to the initial sample. These findings indicate that, despite some microstructural differences, the overall strength of the 800-30 sample remains largely comparable to that of the initial sample. Nevertheless, the YS and UTS values of the 800-30 sample exhibit substantial reductions, with YS decreasing by 74.7 % and 71.3 %, and by 55.8 % relative to the rolled, 600-30, and 700-30 samples, respectively. Similarly, UTS declined by 56.5 %, 53 %, and 33.7 % compared to these samples. This decline in strength can be primarily attributed to the decomposition of martensite islands, the removal of the zigzag, shear, and deformed bands, a marked decrease in dislocation density, and a higher fraction of grains with elevated Schmidt Factors in the 800-30 sample compared to the rolled, 600-30, and 700-30 samples. As shown in  Fig. 13 , annealing at 600 °C led to an increase in absorbed energy compared to the rolled sample, primarily as a result of enhanced ductility. However, upon reaching 700 °C, a decline in absorbed energy was noted, which can be attributed to the reduction in strength relative to the 600-30 sample. Conversely, after annealing at 800 °C, the absorbed energy rose once again, driven by the substantial improvement in ductility. As illustrated in  Fig. 12 , the 800-30 sample displays the yield point phenomenon (YPP). This phenomenon arises from the interaction between dissolved carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) atoms with mobile dislocations during plastic deformation. During tensile testing, C and N atoms diffuse toward mobile dislocations, momentarily impeding their motion. As deformation continues, these dislocations experience repeated pinning and unpinning due to the presence of dissolved atoms. This cyclic obstruction and subsequent release of dislocations lead to a serrated or intermittent flow pattern in the stress-strain curve. When the sample is annealed at 800 °C, the martensite islands fully decompose, enhancing the probability of the yield point phenomenon. Moreover, dislocation density plays a crucial role in this effect, as a high density of dislocations and an increased fraction of grain boundaries tend to eliminate the yield point phenomenon [ 32 , 51 , 52 ]. In the case of the 800-30 sample, the combined effects of recovery and recrystallization lead to a reduced dislocation density and a lower fraction of grain boundaries, attributed to grain growth. This condition amplifies the intensity of the serrated flow behavior.

The results indicate that the 600-30 and 700-30 samples possess superior mechanical properties compared to the other tested samples.  Table 3 
                          summarizes the mechanical properties obtained from the engineering stress-strain curves of AISI 430 ferritic stainless steel fabricated using thermomechanical processing. As depicted in  Table 3 , the samples subjected to asymmetric rolling followed by annealing exhibit an exceptional balance of strength and ductility. Moreover, given the simplicity of the asymmetric rolling process and the ability to achieve enhanced mechanical properties with a strain level below 0.7, this technique distinctly outperforms other conventional processing methods.

Fig. 12  indicates noticeable variations in the work-hardening rates of the samples. To quantify these differences, the work-hardening rates (Θ = dσ/dε) were determined for the initial, rolled, 600-30, 700-30, and 800-30 samples, with the results displayed in  Fig. 15 
                         . Overall, the work-hardening behavior of the samples, with the exception of the rolled and 800-30 samples, exhibits a conventional hardening trend. As shown in  Fig. 15 , the as-received sample had the lowest initial work-hardening rate. Furthermore, a three-stage work-hardening response was observed, attributed to the low initial dislocation density in the sheet. Following asymmetric rolling, the initial work-hardening rate reached its peak among all samples, and due to the significant rise in dislocation density, the hardening process was confined to a single stage. However, annealing the rolled sample led to a reduction in dislocation density in the 600-30 and 700-30 samples, which not only decreased the slope of the work-hardening rate but also reintroduced multiple hardening stages.

In the 800-30 sample, following the initial work-hardening phase, a relative rise in the work-hardening rate occurred due to the onset of the yield point phenomenon. Once this phenomenon subsided, the material exhibited second and third-stage work-hardening behavior, which aligns with expectations given the influence of recrystallization and the associated reduction in dislocation density.  Fig. 15  clearly illustrates that as the annealing temperature increased, the work-hardening capacity improved. This trend is primarily driven by a decrease in dislocation density and an increase in grain size.

sections.heading: Fracture morphology
paragraphs:
Fig. 16 
                          displays the fracture surfaces of the annealed samples following tensile testing. The significant presence of dimples across all annealed samples suggests that ductile fracture is the predominant failure mechanism. In dual-phase steels, ductile fracture progresses through three stages: void nucleation, void growth, and void coalescence. Void nucleation in these steels can occur via several mechanisms, including decohesion at α/α′ interfaces, decohesion at α′/α' interfaces, decohesion at α/α boundaries, and cracking within the α′ phase [ 59 ]. In the as-received sample, void formation on the fracture surface was primarily driven by decohesion at α/α′ interfaces. This decohesion arises due to the mechanical property mismatch between ferrite and martensite. The greater plasticity of ferrite relative to martensite results in strain incompatibility at their interface, ultimately leading to void formation. Previous studies have also documented the presence of voids associated with decohesion at ferrite/martensite interfaces. In the fracture surface of the 600-30 sample, multiple-layered cracks are evident, indicating reduced ductility compared to the other annealed sheets.  Fig. 16 (b) reveals that the 600-30 sample exhibits a non-uniform fracture morphology, which corresponds to its heterogeneous microstructure. However, this sample underwent sufficient plastic deformation before failure, likely due to the beneficial impact of recovery on its ductility. After annealing at 700 °C for 30 min, the fracture surface became more uniform, with dimples displaying a more uniform distribution ( Fig. 16 (d)). Meanwhile, the 800-30 sample's fracture surface ( Fig. 16 (f)) demonstrates a highly homogeneous arrangement of dimples, deeper dimples, and an increased dimple count. This confirms that ductile fracture remains the predominant failure mechanism. Moreover, martensite islands are no longer present on the fracture surface, and the overall dimple size has considerably decreased.  Fig. 16 (e) and (f) illustrate that the 800-30 sample exhibits no signs of layered cracking, suggesting superior ductility compared to the 600-30 and 700-30 samples. The progressive changes in fracture surface morphology with rising annealing temperatures highlight key microstructural modifications. Elevated annealing temperatures facilitate recrystallization, the decomposition of martensite islands, and the development of new ferrite grains, resulting in a more uniform grain structure. This structural refinement minimizes stress concentration sites and enhances overall ductility. The increased dimple count, greater dimple depth, and improved dimple distribution further indicate enhanced void nucleation and growth mechanisms during plastic deformation. These observations underscore the strong correlation between annealing parameters, microstructural development, and fracture behavior, offering critical insights for optimizing the mechanical properties of ferritic stainless steel. Considering all the experimental findings, the 600-30 sample demonstrates the most favorable mechanical properties relative to the 700-30 and 800-30 samples, positioning it as the most optimal material in this study. This preference is based on its combination of outstanding tensile strength and sufficient ductility.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This research examined the influence of annealing at 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C for 30 min on the microstructure, texture, and mechanical characteristics of asymmetrically rolled AISI 430 alloy, yielding the following key findings: 
                         
                            1. 
                            At 600 °C, recrystallization and recovery were minimal. Increasing the annealing temperature to 700 °C resulted in a slight enhancement of these processes, with the fraction of recrystallized areas being four times greater than in the 600-30 sample. At 800 °C, complete recrystallization occurred, leading to the decomposition of martensite islands and the formation of equiaxed ferrite grains. Furthermore, the presence of martensite islands in the rolled sample contributed to a well-distributed and homogeneous microstructure in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions after annealing. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            In the 600-30 sample, the mid-thickness region exhibited a dominant α-fiber texture, primarily concentrated around the {112}<110> component, while the near-surface regions displayed a shear texture associated with the Rotated Cube Y component. As the annealing temperature increased to 800 °C, a well-developed recrystallized γ-fiber texture, along with a strong α-fiber texture, emerged in both the mid-thickness and near-surface regions. The higher shear strain in the 600-30 sample led to the formation of a more pronounced shear component near the surface, delaying the development of recrystallized texture in this region compared to the mid-thickness. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            As the annealing temperature increased, the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) also rose. Moreover, a notable increase in the fraction of CSL boundaries was detected, particularly for Σ3 and Σ13b, which showed a more significant growth with higher temperatures. In contrast, the 800-30 sample exhibited a reduction in Σ11 boundaries due to the decomposition of martensite islands, distinguishing it from the other samples. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            Elevated annealing temperatures enhanced hardness uniformity across the sheet thickness. Increasing the annealing temperature led to a reduction in UTS and YS values while promoting greater ductility. This behavior was influenced by several factors, including the softening and decomposition of martensite islands, the removal of zigzag, shear, and deformed bands, a decrease in dislocation density and work hardening, variations in grain size and Schmidt factor, and changes in texture. Moreover, the ability of the material to undergo work hardening improved with higher annealing temperatures. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            Among the analyzed samples, the 600-30 sample demonstrated the most favorable mechanical properties compared to the 700-30 and 800-30 samples. This superiority was attributed to its combination of high strength and sufficient ductility.
